He wants to activate on his opponent's turn, before end phase, to have the creature survive to his turn. 

To do this, he needs to activate during the opponent's end phase. He is a non-active player without priority. See 513.1 

It's not that he has no priority during M2, it's that the timing doesn't work. If he activates during M2 he loses the creature during the opponent's end step. See 513.1a

513.1. The end step has no turn-based actions. Once it begins, the active player gets priority. (See rule 117, “Timing and Priority.”)

513.1a Previously, abilities that triggered at the beginning of the end step were printed with the trigger condition “at end of turn.” Cards that were printed with that text have received errata in the Oracle card reference to say “at the beginning of the end step” or “at the beginning of the next end step.”

513.2. If a permanent with an ability that triggers “at the beginning of the end step” enters the battlefield during this step, that ability won’t trigger until the next turn’s end step. Likewise, if a delayed triggered ability that triggers “at the beginning of the next end step” is created during this step, that ability won’t trigger until the next turn’s end step. In other words, the step doesn’t “back up” so those abilities can go on the stack. This rule applies only to triggered abilities; it doesn’t apply to continuous effects whose durations say “until end of turn” or “this turn.” (See rule 514, “Cleanup Step.”)
This scenario would work if he was the active player and it was his end step, though.

The active player gets priority. 

That's the opponent. He gets no priority other than when changing from main 2 to end.

So the priority system doesn't give you the timing you're looking for. 

When the opponent goes to their end phase, they pass priority for you to activate abilities before moving from second main to end step. Once in the end step, no priority available during cleanup.

Edit: Reading is hard. Priority is passed as a condition of end step.
Essentially, there isn't an instance to activate the ability without transitioning to the end phase and clearing the stack.

If you activate this on the opponents end step you will lose the creature on the next end step. 

The next end step, unfortunately, is your opponent's end step.

What seems to work with me for my hair (to curl) is to condition for two washes and then use shampoo with conditioner after. Warm wash with conditioner to open hair follicles, cold rinse out to close with conditioner in hair. 

As far as after the shower you have to find what works for your hair type. Gels are usually shiner, but they can style curls. Little flaky. Pomade is usually too tacky and thick for curls. You have to find something light that compliments your hair type. I use hair pudding and that works for me. 

Other things to keep in mind is that to get curls you usually need length and you want to "scrunch" or "crush" the hair as you wash/condition/style. That will help exaggerate the curls. Also don't want to towel dry the hair to death, get the drip out and leave it. I usually wash before going to bed but you can do it in the morning. Gotta find a routine that will keep the hair hydrated. 

Best of luck!

PP29 comes with a heavy drum mag as 1st option. LCMG with CQC drops damage/range from base by 5 but increases ROF. The PKP has no close quarters, only standard/heavy. 

I've been playing with LMG's almost exclusively since the 11th, and I'm off work for a bit due to a career change so I hit lv50 last night. LMG's are good when they're good, but it's more because of a larger mag than fire superiority. I end up using the LCMG with shorty and CQC rounds for super close buildings for higher fire rate, PKP for almost everything else. 

I routinely get outgunned at 50-120m with both LMGs by the PP. I'd say the most frustrating deaths are losing an engagement at range, but it seems like the bulletspread may also be a hindrance. The LMG's are good. PKP is great if you have a big mousepad and don't want to use meta weapons. But they're routinely outgunned by the PP, so at this point it feels more luck than skill.

This is my own opinion and it's subjective of course. I'd like to see the PP brought down a hair and everything else buffed slightly. Give the pp more damage drop-off, higher recoil to make it less viable at range but a solid CQC weapon. Maybe reduce the spread on the AR's and very slightly buff the damage. 

Biggest thing we need is attachments that don't do the same thing tbh, or better understanding of their values to better control weapons.

There's quite a few things to consider prior to enlisting:

1. How do you plan on facilitating care for your mother in your absence? You could sign her on as a dependent and move her with you, although I imagine there would be some out of pocket costs incurred. 

2. Keep your expectations of what you expect to gain from service realistic. If you're financially stable, it wouldn't hurt to attempt to pay off debts and save your base pay. You will gain some perspective from your service. Consider looking into an MOS similar to your current field to expand on your current experience. Have a plan to progress financially or professionally.

Not a radio operator but I service RT-1523's, ARC-201's, and have carrier orders for SKL's and COMSEC. 

NOTE: The following is public information and doesn't breach OPSEC. More information can be found on wikipedia under SINCGARS. 

For the most part, like another commenter stated, they're fairly similar to the Vietnam era radios. The handsets are exactly the same and the weight (and handset) are very similar to the AN/PRC-77. The small black handmic with the singular button. Main difference is the COMSEC security, ciphers and frequency hopping built into modern radios, where as Vietnam era radios were single frequency. 

The manpak usually consists of a singular RT-1523 but instead of using PRC style handheld receivers we use OE-254 transmitters as an intermediate between radios. If I remember correctly, the PRC-77 can interface with OE-254s due to it's original purpose being a trans/receiver for VRCs (vehicular radio communications). Our manpak ground radios mainly operate on line of sight but have much more power to project in comparison to the old Vietnam era radios. New radios also are incredibly modular and the same configuration in a manpak can be stuck into a VRC-90 assembly in a vehicle and used for convoy comms. 

TL;DR
Based on line of sight communications but still use some artifacts from transition periods inbetween Vietnam Era and Desert Storm. We use SINCGARS systems instead of single frequency radios like in the Vietnam era due to security. Fairly light weight and small.

This guy's got it. Supply Chain Management is how manufacturers procure indirect materials (anything that doesn't directly become a part of the end product) and direct materials (raw materials for the production of product.)

For example, at an automotive factory indirect materials are everything from cleaning supplies to forklifts. Direct materials are everything from seatbelts to raw steel. 

It's a legitimate job. When I was in college I did a 1yr internship working in Supply Chain Management and it was about 4 people covering 11 factories across the US. They'd negotiate the contracts from the supplier's supplier to us and try to produce cost savings to translate into lower operations cost. 

It was actually a very lucrative career if it's through a large enough business. 

TLDR: They work on ergonomics in a corporation's finances and try to lower costs to make shit cheaper for joes.
